title: Pod hardening, identity and Kubernetes permissions
design_ref: The sandbox node pool and pod hardening; Threat model arrows 3 and 4
purpose: Show that a sandbox holds no Kubernetes credential, runs unprivileged on a read-only filesystem, that its ServiceAccount can do nothing, and that the namespace refuses a privileged pod.

checks.description: the pod opts into the microVM runtime and mounts no ServiceAccount token
checks.because: These fields come straight from the SandboxTemplate; the controller copies them into every pod.

checks.description: the container drops all capabilities, forbids privilege escalation and has a read-only root filesystem
checks.because: Defence in depth: even inside the microVM the pod is hardened as if it were not.

checks.description: the code runs as uid 1000, cannot write to the root filesystem and finds no service-account directory
checks.because: runAsUser, readOnlyRootFilesystem and automountServiceAccountToken=false in the template.

checks.description: the sandbox ServiceAccount can do nothing on the Kubernetes API
checks.because: It has no Role or ClusterRole bound to it.

checks.description: the sandboxes namespace contains no Kubernetes Secret at all
checks.because: Credentials live only in the namespaces of the components that use them.

checks.description: a privileged, host-network pod is refused by Pod Security admission
checks.because: The namespace enforces the Pod Security 'restricted' profile.

checks.description: each platform identity holds only the permissions its job needs
checks.because: The Manager can create claims but not exec; the Router can exec only inside sandboxes; the orchestrator has no Kubernetes access.
